text: A volume is only as safe as its backup. This lesson covers EBS snapshots — what they actually are, why they stay cheap even on a nightly schedule, how to restore one into a usable volume, and why a real backup strategy means scheduling them, not hoping the volume never fails.

aws ec2 create-snapshot takes a point-in-time copy of a volume, and AWS stores it in S3 behind the scenes — you never manage a bucket for it directly, but that's the real storage layer underneath every snapshot you take.

The key word is incremental. The first snapshot of a volume copies every block, but every snapshot after that only copies the blocks that changed since the last one. That's why a nightly schedule doesn't cost anywhere near a full copy each time, even though restoring from any single snapshot still gives you the volume's complete state at that moment, not just the delta it actually stored.

A snapshot isn't directly usable — restoring means creating a brand-new volume from it with create-volume and a snapshot ID. That new volume doesn't have to land in the same Availability Zone as the original, which is exactly how you move data across AZs or recover after one fails: snapshot, then restore into the AZ you actually need.

A single manual snapshot only reflects whatever the volume looked like on the day someone remembered to take it — that's not a strategy. Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager automates the real version: a policy that snapshots tagged volumes on a schedule and expires old ones by retention age, so a recovery point always exists.

That closes out Chapter 3 — buckets, objects, storage classes, versioning, lifecycle rules, access control, EBS volumes, and now snapshots and backup strategy. Next, Chapter 4 moves from storage to networking, starting with VPC fundamentals and CIDR planning: the network your instances actually live inside.
